tip: 'cyn' (before) takes the verb-noun straight on: 'cyn gwneud' = before doing. No 'ing', just the base verb.
Welsh shows possession by stacking words with no 'of': 'brawd fy ffrind' = my friend's brother, literally brother my friend.
'ga i' (may I have) softens the word after it: 'pwdin' turns into 'bwdin'. 'ga i bwdin' = can I have dessert.
The '-wyd' ending makes a past with no stated doer: 'anfonwyd y llythyr' = the letter was sent.
'siarad â' means to speak to: 'siaradodd hi â'r athro' = she spoke to the teacher. 'â' marks who is addressed.
Welsh has no verb 'to have'. 'gan' carries it: 'ganddyn nhw' = they have. 'does dim gardd ganddyn nhw' = they have no garden.
To bring is 'dod â' (come with), so it needs 'â': 'ddaeth e ddim â'i gôt' = he didn't bring his coat.
Past negatives often use 'gwneud' (do) as a helper: 'wnaeth e ddim mwynhau' = he didn't enjoy. The main verb stays as the base 'mwynhau'.
Prepositions take personal endings: 'heb' (without) plus me becomes 'hebdda i' = without me.
Want to do something is 'eisiau' plus the verb-noun, with no word for 'to': 'dw i eisiau dringo' = I want to climb.
'dylen ni' means we should (a form of 'dylwn'). No 'yn' follows, the verb comes straight after: 'dylen ni drio' = we should try.
'wedi' before a verb makes the 'have done' form: 'wedi gorffen' = have finished. Wrap it with 'ddim' to negate.
'faswn i' = I would, the 'would' form of 'bod'. Add 'ddim' for the negative: 'faswn i ddim' = I wouldn't.
Report 'that he' with 'ei fod e': 'mynnodd e ei fod e'n iawn' = he insisted that he was right.
The future 'bydd' often softens to 'fydd' in negatives: 'fydd dim cyfarfod' = there won't be a meeting.
'caf i' means I will get, an irregular future of 'cael' (to get, receive): 'gobeithio y caf i' = I hope I get.
Need to do something is 'angen' plus the verb-noun, nothing between: 'dw i angen prynu' = I need to buy.
'rhaid i' plus a person plus verb-noun means must: 'rhaid i fi orffwys' = I must rest, literally 'necessity to me to rest'.
For going to a person, use 'at' rather than 'i': 'at y deintydd' = to the dentist. 'i' is usually for places, 'at' for people.
The linking word 'a' (and) triggers aspirate mutation, adding an h-sound: 'croesawgar' becomes 'chroesawgar' after 'a'.
'byddwch chi' = you will, for a group or a polite 'you': 'gobeithio byddwch chi'n mwynhau' (hope you'll enjoy).
'mynd â' means to take, literally go with: 'aeth Megan â'r plant' = Megan took the children.
'yn' meaning in triggers nasal mutation and shifts to 'yng': 'Cymru' becomes 'Nghymru', giving 'yng Nghymru' = in Wales.
'pe gallwn i' means if I could, the 'could' form of 'gallu' (to be able): 'pe gallwn i goginio' (if I could cook).
'cwrdd' takes the linker 'â' for the person you meet: 'cwrddais i â ffrind' (I met a friend).
'trowch' is a command with the '-wch' ending, used for a group or someone formal. To a single friend you'd say 'tro'.
'mynd' (to go) is irregular in the past: 'aeth' = went, not 'mynddodd'. 'aeth y bachgen' = the boy went.
Preference is shown with 'gan': 'roedd yn well ganddo' = he preferred it, literally it was better with him.
In reported speech, that is carried by 'fod', a softened 'bod': 'gwyddai hi fod y gwaith' = she knew that the work was hard.
'yn arfer' plus a verb means used to as a habit: 'roedd hi'n arfer chwarae' = she used to play.
